description: The guru, unable to bear the seeker's longing, comes and shows his own form; then the six supports, the fifty-one letters and all the principles are burnt, and the heart stands empty.
The Lord abides like the inner light of a ruby.
Gazing and gazing, the bliss that gives light is seen straight at the forehead.
The unceasing sleep of Śiva-yoga: senses burnt away, sleeping without sleeping, in bliss.
The bliss makes one stagger and dance like a drunkard (Pattirakiriyār 218).
notes: Checked in the local e-text (couplet 218); no separate teaching entry.

description: Having gone above the crown, the high open space is seen (Kuṭampai 11).
notes: Checked in the local e-text; the second half-line is obscure.

description: Binding the breath, the body does not perish for a thousand years (TM 722); grey hair and wrinkles perish and the body becomes like collyrium (TM 727). The texts' claims.

The eight great powers (aṭṭamā citti) claimed for the Siddhars; listed by Tāyumāṉavar with taming beasts, transmutation, invisibility, perpetual youth, entering another body, walking on water and sitting in fire — all ranked below stilling the mind.
Bogar's own account of travelling to China and of flight through the air (the text's claim).
In the tradition, at Tiruvoṟṟiyūr Paṭṭiṉattār had boys cover him with a basket; when it was lifted he had vanished and a liṅga stood in his place.
notes: The tradition's account (hagiography), not a verse of the songs.

description: In the tradition, when Paṭṭiṉattār was condemned to the stake at Ujjain the stake burst into flame.
The tradition holds that the Siddhars remain present in their samādhi shrines and hill retreats and appear to devotees.
